## Defining flexibility

[The previous page](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd) drew a curve with "flexibility" on the
horizontal axis and left the word undefined. It has to be defined, because the whole of model
selection consists of moving along that axis, and you cannot move along an axis you cannot
measure.

The intuitive definition, counting the parameters, works for the models marine scientists learn
first and fails for almost everything else. A random forest with 500 trees has hundreds of
thousands of thresholds and is *less* prone to overfitting than one tree with 400. A ridge
regression has exactly as many coefficients as an unpenalised one and behaves as though it has
a quarter as many.

This page is about what the axis really measures, and it ends with the most direct
demonstration in the course of why it matters.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs.qmd >}}

## The idea

Complexity is best understood as **how many different datasets a model could fit equally
well**. A straight line can be dragged around by two numbers; there are many surveys it cannot
describe at all. A tree with one station per leaf can describe any survey whatsoever, including
one where abundance is assigned by dice.

That is the sense in which complexity is dangerous. A model that could fit anything tells you
nothing when it fits your data, because fitting your data was never in doubt.

The useful currency is **effective degrees of freedom**: roughly, how many independent
quantities the model is actually estimating. For an ordinary linear model that is the number of
coefficients. For everything else it is smaller than the raw count, sometimes far smaller, and
it can be a fraction.

| Family | The knob | What raises complexity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linear regression | Number of terms | Polynomials, interactions, dummy levels |
| Ridge / lasso | Penalty $\lambda$ | *Lowering* λ |
| Decision tree | Depth, `minbucket`, `cp` | Deeper, smaller leaves |
| Random forest | `mtry`, `min_n` | Smaller leaves; **not** more trees |
| Boosting | Trees × depth × learning rate | More rounds, deeper trees, larger steps |
| k-nearest neighbours | *k* | *Lowering* k |
| Neural network | Layers, units | Wider, deeper, longer training |

Two rows of that table are backwards from the naive reading, and both catch people out. In
ridge and in k-NN, the knob you turn *up* is the one that makes the model simpler. And adding
trees to a random forest does not add complexity at all; it averages more copies of the same
complexity, which is why a forest of 5,000 trees does not overfit more than one of 500.

### Effective degrees of freedom, measured

Ridge regression makes this concrete. The coefficients are all still there, twelve of them,
but the penalty stops them moving freely, and the number of effectively free directions falls
continuously as λ rises.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

d <- survey |>
  select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3,
         salinity_psu, substrate, season) |>
  drop_na()

X <- scale(model.matrix(
  ~ depth_m + I(depth_m^2) + temperature_c + I(temperature_c^2) +
    chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season,
  data = d
)[, -1])

singular_values <- svd(X)$d

effective_df <- function(lambda) sum(singular_values^2 / (singular_values^2 + lambda))

tibble(lambda = c(0, 1, 10, 100, 500, 1000, 5000)) |>
  mutate(`effective degrees of freedom` = map_dbl(lambda, effective_df)) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Python

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()

columns = ["abundance", "depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3",
           "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season"]
d = survey[columns].dropna()

design = pd.get_dummies(
    d.assign(depth_sq=d["depth_m"] ** 2,
             temperature_sq=d["temperature_c"] ** 2)
     .drop(columns="abundance"),
    drop_first=True,
).astype(float)

X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(design)

singular_values = np.linalg.svd(X, compute_uv=False)

def effective_df(lam):
    return (singular_values ** 2 / (singular_values ** 2 + lam)).sum()

lambdas = [0, 1, 10, 100, 500, 1000, 5000]
pd.DataFrame({
    "lambda": lambdas,
    "effective degrees of freedom": [effective_df(lam) for lam in lambdas],
}).round(3)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-edf
#| fig-cap: "Effective degrees of freedom of a twelve-coefficient ridge regression, against the penalty λ. The model always has twelve coefficients. At λ = 1000 it is estimating the equivalent of about four free quantities; by λ = 100,000 it is estimating almost nothing and predicts the mean everywhere."
#| fig-alt: "A curve descending from left to right on axes of lambda from 0.01 to 100,000 on a logarithmic scale against effective degrees of freedom from zero to twelve. The curve is flat at twelve until lambda reaches about 1, then falls steadily, passing eight at lambda 100 and four at lambda 1000, and flattening towards zero beyond lambda 20,000. A dotted horizontal line marks twelve, the number of coefficients the model has throughout."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
tibble(lambda = exp(seq(log(0.01), log(1e5), length.out = 200))) |>
  mutate(edf = map_dbl(lambda, effective_df)) |>
  ggplot(aes(lambda, edf)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = ncol(X), linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
  labs(x = "λ (log scale)", y = "Effective degrees of freedom",
       title = "Twelve coefficients, and between zero and twelve of them free",
       subtitle = "Dotted line: the number of coefficients, which never changes")
```

This is what [MAP estimation](../04-how-algorithms-learn/map-and-priors.qmd) was doing when the
prior pulled coefficients towards zero. The parameters remain in the model; what shrinks is how
much independent information each is allowed to carry. Complexity is not a count of parameters
but a measure of how free they are.

## Worked example

Here is the demonstration. We will take three genuine predictors and add columns of `rnorm()`:
not weak predictors, not proxies, but *pure random numbers generated after the fact and
known to contain nothing at all*. Then watch what the model reports about itself.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: noise-experiment
set.seed(503)
split <- initial_split(d, prop = 0.75)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

rmse_of <- function(observed, predicted) sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2))

with_noise <- function(k) {
  set.seed(1000 + k)
  noise_train <- matrix(rnorm(nrow(train) * k), nrow(train))
  noise_test  <- matrix(rnorm(nrow(test) * k), nrow(test))
  colnames(noise_train) <- colnames(noise_test) <-
    if (k > 0) paste0("noise", seq_len(k)) else character(0)

  a <- bind_cols(train |> select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3),
                 as_tibble(noise_train))
  b <- bind_cols(test  |> select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3),
                 as_tibble(noise_test))

  fit <- lm(abundance ~ ., data = a)
  tibble(
    `noise columns`   = k,
    `training R²`     = summary(fit)$r.squared,
    `training RMSE`   = rmse_of(a$abundance, predict(fit, a)),
    `test RMSE`       = rmse_of(b$abundance, suppressWarnings(predict(fit, b)))
  )
}

noise_results <- map_dfr(c(0, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, nrow(train) - 1), with_noise)

noise_results |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Python

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, root_mean_squared_error
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

train, test = train_test_split(d, train_size=0.75, random_state=503)

real = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3"]

def with_noise(k):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1000 + k)
    names = [f"noise{i + 1}" for i in range(k)]

    a = pd.concat([train[real].reset_index(drop=True),
                   pd.DataFrame(rng.standard_normal((len(train), k)),
                                columns=names)], axis=1)
    b = pd.concat([test[real].reset_index(drop=True),
                   pd.DataFrame(rng.standard_normal((len(test), k)),
                                columns=names)], axis=1)

    # Once k reaches n - 1 the design is saturated. lm() reports NA for the
    # coefficients it cannot identify; LinearRegression solves the same system
    # by least norm instead, so the numbers differ where R prints NA.
    fit = LinearRegression().fit(a, train["abundance"])
    return {
        "noise columns": k,
        "training R²": r2_score(train["abundance"], fit.predict(a)),
        "training RMSE": root_mean_squared_error(train["abundance"], fit.predict(a)),
        "test RMSE": root_mean_squared_error(test["abundance"], fit.predict(b)),
    }

pd.DataFrame([with_noise(k) for k in
              [0, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, len(train) - 1]]).round(3)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-noise
#| fig-cap: "Training R² and test RMSE against the number of pure-noise columns added to three real predictors, on 540 training stations. Training R² climbs from 0.137 to exactly 1.000. Test RMSE climbs from 4.39 to 185, against a response whose largest observed value is 40."
#| fig-alt: "Two stacked panels sharing a horizontal axis of noise columns from zero to 539 on a square-root scale. The upper panel shows training R-squared rising from 0.14 at zero columns, slowly at first and then steeply, reaching exactly 1.0 at 539. The lower panel, on a logarithmic vertical axis, shows test RMSE almost flat near 4.4 up to about 25 columns, then rising through 5, 6 and 9.5, and jumping to 185 at 539 columns."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
p1 <- ggplot(noise_results, aes(`noise columns`, `training R²`)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = ml_palette[["orange"]]) +
  geom_point(size = 2, colour = ml_palette[["orange"]]) +
  scale_x_sqrt(breaks = c(0, 25, 100, 200, 400, 539)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Training R²",
       title = "What the model says about itself")

p2 <- ggplot(noise_results, aes(`noise columns`, `test RMSE`)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) +
  geom_point(size = 2, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) +
  scale_x_sqrt(breaks = c(0, 25, 100, 200, 400, 539)) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Columns of pure random noise added", y = "Test RMSE (log scale)",
       title = "What it does on new stations")

p1 / p2
```

## The cost of 539 noise columns

With no noise columns the model explains 13.7% of the training variance and scores 4.39 on new
stations. Adding 539 columns of `rnorm()` takes the training R² to **1.000** and the test RMSE
to **185**.

Sit with the first of those numbers. A perfect fit. Not 0.98 but 1.000, and a training RMSE of
exactly zero. Any reader shown that model's summary, without being told where the columns came
from, would conclude that abundance on this shelf is completely determined and the study is
finished.

The mechanism is simple arithmetic and worth stating because it is the general case, not a
quirk: with 540 training stations and 540 coefficients, the model has exactly enough freedom to
pass through every point. There is no residual left for it to report. The R² is 1 not because
the model found something but because it ran out of data to be wrong about.

Two more readings matter.

**The damage starts long before the collapse.** At 25 noise columns, 29 parameters on 540
stations and a ratio most people would call comfortable, the training R² has already risen from
0.137 to 0.177 and the test RMSE has begun to drift up from 4.39 to 4.50. Every junk column you
add buys a little training fit and costs a little real performance, from the very first one.
There is no threshold below which extra variables are free.

**This is what "more data" means.** The problem here is not 539 columns; it is 539 columns
against 540 stations. The same 539 columns with 50,000 stations would be almost harmless. What
governs overfitting is the ratio, which is why sample size and complexity have to be discussed
together and why a survey design question is also a modelling question.

::: {.callout-warning}
R² never falls when you add a predictor. Not "rarely" but never, as a matter of algebra, however
irrelevant the predictor is. This makes R² unusable for comparing models with different numbers
of terms, and it is why adjusted R², AIC and cross-validation exist. If you have ever added a
variable, seen R² rise, and taken that as evidence the variable matters, this table is the
counter-example: it happens with random numbers, every time.
:::

## Limits of counting parameters

**Parameter counts do not compare across families.** The 540-parameter model above is a
catastrophe. A random forest here has hundreds of thousands of thresholds and is fine. The
numbers are not on the same scale and should never be compared as though they were; the only
comparison that means anything is performance on held-out data.

**Effective degrees of freedom is not always computable.** The tidy formula used above exists
for ridge and other linear smoothers. For trees, forests and boosting there is no equivalent,
and the honest position is that their complexity can be *ordered* by turning a knob but not
*measured* on a common scale.

**Complexity is not the only route to overfitting.** A simple model fitted after you have
looked at the data twenty times and chosen the variables that worked is overfitted too, and
nothing in its parameter count reveals it. This is selection bias rather than model complexity,
it is invisible to every diagnostic on this page, and
[section 2](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd) named it as one of the four kinds of
leakage.

**Some complexity is required.** Nothing here argues for the simplest model available. The
[previous page's](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd) seven-leaf tree was underfitted, and a
model too rigid to represent a thermal optimum will mislead you as reliably as one that fits
noise, just more quietly, and with better-looking diagnostics.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points

- Complexity means **how many different datasets the model could fit**, not how many parameters
  it has.
- **Effective degrees of freedom** is the useful measure. A twelve-coefficient ridge model has
  twelve coefficients at every λ, and about four free directions at λ = 1000.
- Two knobs run backwards: raising λ in ridge and raising *k* in k-NN both make the model
  *simpler*. Adding trees to a forest changes complexity not at all.
- Adding 539 columns of pure random noise to 540 training stations produced a training R² of
  exactly **1.000** and a test RMSE of **185**.
- R² cannot decrease when a predictor is added, whatever the predictor is. It is not a
  model-comparison statistic.

:::

## Try it yourself

1. Re-run the noise experiment with 200 noise columns but only 100 training stations. The ratio
   is worse than any row in the table: what happens to the coefficient table, and what does
   `lm()` do when it runs out of degrees of freedom entirely?
2. Fit ridge regression at λ = 1000 to the 539-noise-column design matrix. Effective degrees of
   freedom says it should behave like a four-parameter model. Does its test RMSE agree, and what
   does that say about the difference between having parameters and using them?
